text.p: Germany's top law enforcer said on Tuesday the Red Army Faction (RAF) left-wing guerrilla group, whose name struck fear into the heart of the establishment in the 1970s and 1980s, was now "almost insignificant".
Some 50 people were killed in the war of assassinations and kidnappings which the RAF, once known as the Baader-Meinhof gang, waged on the German political and business elite.
Now, with most of its members dead, jailed, or submerged in bourgeois anonymity, prosecutors are at last starting to think the unthinkable -- that the RAF may be dead.

Federal Prosecutor Kay Nehm told an annual news conference in Karlsruhe that the threat from the RAF had faded and that his office was focusing on attacks which took place in the late 1980s which remained unsolved.

He also conceded for the first time that it was not yet clear whether charges would be pressed against Christoph Seidler, chief suspect in the 1989 RAF murder of Deutsche Bank chief executive Alfred Herrhausen.
Seidler gave himself up last year. He says he is innocent, and two courts have said there is not enough evidence to keep him in investigative custody.
The attack on Herrhausen was one of a series which forced German banks and companies to turn their headquarters into virtual fortresses.

But there have been no fatal attacks attributed to the RAF since the 1991 murder of Detlef Rohwedder, head of the Treuhand agency which was privatising East Germany's state industry, only six months after the euphoria of German unification.
Messages from the group have become rare, and its eight members left in jail all now reject political violence.
A letter published in December and believed to be from the RAF's current leaders said that "the RAF's concept is outdated" and that there could be no "modified version of the old one".

Nehm said the role of thorn in the German establishment's side had now been taken over by a number of smaller but less extreme groups, such as the militants who have sabotaged train lines to protest against the storage of nuclear waste.

The weekly Der Spiegel said criminal investigators were discreetly telling companies they could relax some of their security precautions as RAF attacks aimed at individuals rather than property now seemed unlikely.
Nehm vowed, however, that the search for the perpetrators of unsolved assassinations would go on. Of six fatal RAF attacks between 1985 and 1991, only one has led to a conviction.
Investigations were hampered by the fact that East Germany's Ministry for State Security (Stasi) gave shelter to 10 RAF guerrillas in the 1980s.

Since unification, many of those guerrillas have been jailed. Later this month, the former West German investigators may get some satisfaction when Stasi officers responsible for taking in RAF members go on trial in Berlin.
